合抱之木產於鄧林，培養之久而後可以成其材；連城之璧出于荆山，追琢之精而後可以就其器。况夫國家生賢關於氣運，士子力學由於積累，非偶然也。洪惟我朝太祖、太宗二聖相承，締造家邦，誕敷文治，以啓億萬載之太平。仁宗皇帝恢弘治道，謹科額以抑僥倖；今上皇帝繼體守文，簡生徒以勵士風。經綸密勿，久而益隆，得人之盛，超漢、唐而軼虞、周，其來尚矣。乃宣德癸丑，時當大比，行在禮部尚書臣濙以聞。上命臣淮、臣直典持文衡，臣恬、臣永清、臣茂弘、臣英、臣賜、臣潤生、臣琬、臣暹同司考校，臣濙提挈
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Trees a full arm-span around grow in the Forest of Deng, yet only after long cultivation can they be made into useful timber; jade disks worth a string of cities come from Mount Jing, yet only after refined carving and polishing can they be fashioned into ritual vessels. How much more so is this true of the state's producing men of worth, which depends upon the cycle of destiny, and of scholars' diligent study, which relies upon gradual accumulation—none of it is accidental. Reflecting deeply upon our dynasty, the two sagely sovereigns Grand Progenitor (Taizu) and Grand Ancestor (Taizong) succeeded one another, founding the dynastic state and broadly spreading civil governance so as to inaugurate ten-thousand-myriad years of great peace. Emperor Renzong expanded the Way of governance and strictly regulated examination quotas in order to curb opportunistic fortune-seeking; the reigning Emperor, succeeding to the body of the state and upholding the civil order, selects government students with care in order to encourage the ethos of the literati. Their statecraft has been assiduous and thorough, growing ever more flourishing with time, so that the abundance of capable men obtained surpasses that of the Han and Tang and outstrips that of Yu and Zhou—its origins go back a long way indeed. Now, in the guichou year of the Xuande reign (1433), when the time came for the great triennial examination, your servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, Minister of Rites in the Auxiliary Administration, memorialized to inform the Throne. His Majesty commanded your servants [Huang] Huai 黃淮 and [Wang] Zhi 王直 to take charge of the literary balance as Examiners; your servants [Chen] Tian 陳恬, [Li] Yongqing 李永清, [Chen] Maohong 陳茂弘, [Wang] Ying 王英, [Huang] Ci 黃賜, [Lin] Runsheng 林潤生, [Zheng] Wan 鄭琬, and [Wu] Xian 吳暹 to serve jointly as Associate Examiners; while your servant [Hu] Ying took charge of upholding…

translation_en: … the overarching direction, while those charged with surveillance and inspection were the Investigating Censors Your Servant Ao [Wang Ao 王翺] and Your Servant Jun [Jiang Jun 姜駿]. The functionaries of the inner and outer courts received the imperial command with utmost diligence. Scholars from all quarters who came accompanied by the account-reporting officials numbered fourteen hundred in all, and those who stood out from the crowd like an awl's tip piercing a bag were one hundred men. Their names have been registered in this minor record in full accordance with precedent. Those whose names are inscribed herein are refined and numerous—all lofty timber from the Forest of Deng and two-handed jade disks from Mount Jing, fit to serve as pillars and beams for the high court and as jade libation ladles for the pure ancestral temple. How grand indeed has been the way their talents were perfected and their vessels fashioned! Soon their names will be presented to the Heavenly Archive, and they will answer the policy question in the Great Court; receiving pure ranks and generous stipends, they will repeatedly enjoy distinguished promotion—the pinnacle of honor and good fortune! Yet they ought to reflect that to find oneself in an era of flourishing excellence is truly a rare encounter across the ages and a fine opportunity to devote oneself to service. Let them ever more firmly cultivate their conduct and principles and grandly unfold their talents and plans, so that their achievements become renowned in their own time and their fame and luster flow throughout the universe. Thus they may perhaps not fail the supreme grace with which the Sacred Dynasty has nurtured them, nor fail the substantive learning that illuminates fundamental principles and applies them to practical use—would that not be magnificent! translation_en:
First Session

Four Books
1. "If the superior man abandons humaneness, how can he fulfill that name? The superior man does not, even for the space of a single meal, act contrary to humaneness." (Analects 4.5)
2. "In practicing ordinary virtues and being cautious in ordinary words, when there is any deficiency, he dares not but exert himself; when there is a surplus, he dares not exhaust it. His words correspond to his actions, and his actions correspond to his words; how could the superior man not be earnestly sincere!" (Doctrine of the Mean 13)
3. "What Yu did in guiding the waters was to guide them where no Forceful Action was needed. If wise men also conduct affairs without Forceful Action, then their wisdom too will be great." (Mencius 4B.26)

Classic of Changes (Yi)
1. "Modesty (Qian): honored and yet shining forth, lowly and yet not to be surpassed—such is the consummation of the superior man." (Hexagram 15, Tuanzhuan)
2. "The wind moves above the earth: the image of Contemplation (Guan). Thus the ancient kings visited the regions of the world, contemplated the people, and established instruction." (Hexagram 20, Xiangzhuan)
3. "Heaven is one, earth is two; heaven is three, earth is four; heaven is five, earth is six; heaven is seven, earth is eight; heaven is nine, earth is ten." (Xici shang 9)
4. "The Changes is that by which the sages fathomed the deepest depths and investigated the subtlest springs of things." (Xici shang 10)

Classic of Documents (Shu)
1. "The Emperor thereupon composed a song, saying: 'Stand in awe of the Mandate of Heaven, at every moment and in every subtle incipient sign.' Then he sang: 'When the legs and arms rejoice, the head rises up, and all the official works flourish!'" ("Yi and Ji")
2. "As if protecting a newborn infant, then the people will be peaceful and well-governed." ("Announcement to Kang")

非道之所存也。子游述夫子之言曰：「君子學道則愛人，小人學道則易使。」宜若涉於淺近，且所學則一，而致用不同，何與？抑其分有高下，而學亦有小大精粗之異與？《中庸》一書，子思子憂道學失傳而作。然其所憂，與君子小人之所學同與？否與？其書自戒慎恐懼，推而至於篤恭而天下平；《大學》則自格致誠正，以至於脩齊治平。平治天下，本無二道，節目次第，彼此各異，其說安在？諸君子抱道而来，宜攄素蘊，以究夫明體適用之學。
問：孔子之道，至孟子沒而不傳，宋周子實承之，其道宜無異也。今所著圖、書具在。論者以《太極圖》比《先天圖》，謂太極不如先天之大而詳，先天不如太極之精而約，其說何與？孔子曰：「易有太極。」周子則曰：「無極而太極。」又曰：「太極本無極。」其果同與？又謂「無極之真」，「真」者，何所
translation_en:
…is not where the Way resides? Ziyou 子游 recounted the Master's words, saying, "When the superior man studies the Way, he loves others; when the petty man studies the Way, he is easy to employ." This might seem rather shallow and near at hand; moreover, what they study is one and the same, yet its application differs—why is this? Or is it that because their stations are high or low, their learning also differs in being great or small, refined or coarse? As for the book the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸), Master Zisi 子思子 composed it out of anxiety that the learning of the Way would be lost to transmission. Yet was what he worried about the same as what the superior man and the petty man studied, or not? That book extends from being cautious and apprehensive all the way to being devoutly respectful so that the world is brought to peace; the Great Learning (Daxue 大學), on the other hand, proceeds from investigating things, extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind all the way to cultivating the person, regulating the family, ordering the state, and bringing peace to the world. In bringing peace and order to the world, there are fundamentally not two Ways, yet the specific items and sequences differ from one another—what is the explanation for this? You gentlemen have come embracing the Way; you should set forth your long-accumulated learning so as to thoroughly investigate the study that illuminates fundamental substance and suits practical application.

Question: The Way of Confucius 孔子 ceased to be transmitted after the death of Mencius 孟子, and Master Zhou 周子 [Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤] of the Song truly succeeded to it; their Way ought not to differ. Today the Diagram [Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu shuo 太極圖說)] and the Book [Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu 通書)] that he composed are both extant. Commentators compare the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu 太極圖) with the Diagram of Preceding Heaven (Xiantiantu 先天圖), saying that the Supreme Ultimate is not as grand and detailed as the Preceding Heaven, whereas the Preceding Heaven is not as refined and concise as the Supreme Ultimate—what is the reasoning behind this claim? Confucius said, "In the Changes there is the Supreme Ultimate." …refer to? The Way of the sages consists of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom, yet here he speaks of "benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and correctness" without mentioning ritual propriety or wisdom; Zisi 子思 spoke of centrality and harmony as the substance and function of the Way, yet here he says, "Centrality is harmony, the universal path of all under heaven"; Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) spoke of human nature as good, yet here he speaks of "rigidity, softness, good, evil, and centrality." In all these respects there seem to be differences—why is that? Master Zhang of Hengqu (Zhang Zai 張載) composed the Western Inscription (Ximing 西銘), which Master Zhu (Zhu Xi 朱熹) also revered and trusted, writing commentaries on it alongside the Diagram and the Book to transmit them to posterity. What, in truth, is its main purport? Does it differ from the writings of Master Zhou (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤) or not? Moreover, when it was said that Master Zhang stood alone since Mencius, what exactly was approved in him? If one extends and carries the doctrines of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji 太極) and the Western Inscription to their utmost, what should the result be? I wish to hear the most thorough account of this.

Question: The five tones (wuyin 五音), the six yang pitch-pipes (liulü 六律), and the six yin pitch-pipes (liulü 六呂) are the instruments for creating music. They originated with the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi 黃帝), and later theorists grew ever more precise and detailed. May we hear the meaning behind the establishment of their names? Is there also an explanation for matching the twelve pitch-pipes to the twelve earthly branches (shier chen 十二辰)? Given that the yang and yin pitch-pipes are already divided into yin and yang, why are there also the theories of the three beginnings (sanshi 三始) and the four seasons? There are already five tones; why then are there also the altered宮 (biangong 變宮) and altered徵 (bianzhi 變徵) tones? The twelve pitch-pipes generate one another alternately upward and downward, and the five tones likewise generate one another—what meaning is taken from this? Since there are already full standard tones (zhengsheng 正聲), why are there also derivative tones (zisheng 子聲) and half-tones (bansheng 半聲)? 詳陳之
問易曰聖人之大寶曰位何以守位曰人何以
聚人曰財財用誠國家大計不可忽也漢以
桑弘羊領大農不益賦於民而國用足然當
時有賢良文學之論果孰為得失與唐任劉
晏國用充足而民不困論者謂後之理財者
莫能及其得果安在與宋王安石嘗欲足國

其弊其失果安在與曾子論有人有土有財
而本於德晏之得庶幾於此與其說有可行
於後世與願聞至當之論

律亦有其本與？禮樂之事，諸生所宜知也，其詳陳之。

問：《易》曰：「聖人之大寶曰位，何以守位曰人，何以聚人曰財。」財用誠國家大計，不可忽也。漢以桑弘羊領大農，不益賦於民而國用足；然當時有賢良、文學之論，果孰為得失與？唐任劉晏，國用充足而民不困，論者謂後之理財者莫能及，其得果安在與？宋王安石嘗欲足國裕民，其所行自以為得矣，然卒無效而民受其弊，其失果安在與？曾子論有人、有土、有財，而本於德；晏之得，庶幾於此與？其說有可行於後世與？願聞至當之論。
translation_en:
… establishing the pitch-pipes also has its fundamental basis? Matters of ritual and music are what you students ought to know; set them forth in detail.

Question: The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The great treasure of the sage is called position; that by which he guards his position is called people; that by which he gathers the people is called wealth." Financial administration is truly a great plan of the state and cannot be neglected. The Han dynasty placed Sang Hongyang 桑弘羊 in charge of the Ministry of Agriculture (danong); without increasing taxes on the people, state expenditures were sufficient. Yet at that time there were the arguments of the Worthy and Good (xianliang) and the Literary Scholars (wenxue)—between them, which indeed was right and which wrong? The Tang dynasty employed Liu Yan 劉晏; state finances were abundant and the people were not distressed, so that commentators said later financial administrators could not match him—wherein indeed did his success lie? In the Song dynasty, Wang Anshi 王安石 once wished to enrich the state and bring plenty to the people, and he considered what he carried out to have achieved the mark; yet in the end it had no effect and the people suffered its harms—wherein indeed did his failure lie? Master Zeng (Zengzi 曾子) discussed having people, having territory, and having wealth as being rooted in virtue. Did Liu Yan's success perhaps approximate this? Are his doctrines practicable for later generations? I wish to hear the most fitting discourse on this.

… one often errs on the side of insufficiency; when one has an insufficiency of virtue and yet exerts oneself at it, then one's actions become all the more vigorous, attaining the beauty of steadfast determination, strenuous practice, and shame lest one's person fail to measure up. Because unrestrained speech is easy, one often errs on the side of excess; when one has an excess of speech and yet exercises restraint, then one's caution becomes all the more thorough, avoiding the pitfalls of becoming wild through excessive levity or rambling through excessive verbosity. When speaking with the utmost caution, it is only if one does not speak at all—for if one speaks, one will certainly be mindful of one's actions and in no way contradict them. When acting with vigorous practice, it is only if one does not act at all—for if one acts, one will certainly be mindful of one's words and in no way contravene one's actions [?]. With words corresponding to actions and actions corresponding to words, in being such a gentleman, is he not truly earnest and sincere (zaozao)? For "earnest and sincere" describes an appearance of篤實 (steadfast genuineness) and is an expression of praise. This being so, the reason people fail to become gentlemen is simply because they are unable to exercise utmost care in the ordinary course of words and actions so as to fulfill their reality. Only when one can fulfill the reality can one live up to the name. Furthermore, considering the book Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), it consists of the essential words of the transmission of the Way of the Mind within the Confucian school, written by Master Zisi out of anxiety that the Learning of the Way might lose its transmission. Therefore, at this point he cites the Master's words to clarify the meaning that the Way cannot be departed from for an instant. And what he calls ordinary virtues and ordinary words do not go beyond the affairs of son, minister, younger brother, and friend—turning inward to reprove oneself and cultivate oneself, seeking only to exhaust the Way of conscientiousness and altruism (zhongshu). This chapter builds upon the discussion of the wide-reaching and the hidden (feiyin) in the preceding chapter: ordinary virtues and ordinary words serve to illustrate the smaller aspects of the wide-reaching manifestations, while the principle by which they are so is where the utmost hiddenness resides. Scholars must not fail to examine this.

The great worthy [Mencius] used Yu's conducting of the waters to elucidate the affairs of great wisdom—how profound was his intention in supporting the world and establishing teachings! If one can know its nature, then one will naturally be free from the flaw of artificiality and contrivance that would harm one's wisdom. Its meaning is subtle indeed.

… withdraws in person, yet his Way flourishes, so because he puts himself last, others put him first. This is what is meant by "lowly yet cannot be surpassed." Now, when one occupies an exalted position and is modest, it seems as though he is obscuring himself, yet in the end he truly shines forth; when one abides in a lowly position and is modest, it seems as though he is greatly repressing himself, yet in the end no one can surpass him. These are all the natural effects of the virtue of modesty. Therefore, not only does he obtain good fortune at the beginning, but in the end too there is nothing that is not auspicious; not only does he obtain goodness at the beginning, but in the end too there is nothing that is not good. Could anything be added to this meaning of "having a good end"? Moreover, if we observe the hexagram Modesty (Qian), it has Kun above and Gen below, representing a mountain within the earth. A mountain is supremely high and the earth is supremely low, yet it bends and rests beneath it; this is the image of modesty. King Wen appended his judgment to it, saying: "Modesty: success. The superior man has a good end." In his Commentary on the Judgments (Tuanzhuan), our Master first used the natural Way of Heaven and Earth to make clear that modesty must bring success, and then spoke in detail of the workings of nature and human affairs in order to warn against fullness and encourage modesty; coming to this point, he further elaborated with "illustrious when exalted, and when lowly, cannot be surpassed," so as to show the effect of the superior man's embodying modesty. The sages of earlier and later times have elucidated the meaning of modesty until nothing remains unexpressed.

When the sage ruler composed a song in order to seek good governance, he first gave expression in words to his intention of revering Heaven, and next drew upon the metaphor of sharing a single body to rely upon his ministers. For the sage ruler's intention lay solely in heeding the Mandate of Heaven and being attentive to the moment and the subtle incipient tendencies; thus, in giving form to this in song, how could he not also charge his ministers with the Way of mutuallycompleting one another as parts of a single body? Striking the large drums is a major element of the music; once the sound of the drums rises, it can be known that none of the multitude of sounds fails to be in harmony. When this harmonious and complete music is performed in the temple of our Illustrious Ancestor, the spirit of the Illustrious Ancestor listens to it from the unseen realm with a sense of joy, and hears it amidst its vast presence with a feeling of delight. Is this not how the completeness of the music gladdens the spirit of the former king? Yet since there is that by which the spirit of the former king is gladdened, there must also be that by which his presence is drawn near. Indeed, the one sacrificed to is Cheng Tang, and the one presiding over the sacrifice is Tang's descendant. Standing before him in worship, their sincere intentions mutually respond; performing the music to invoke him, their vital spirits commune and flow together. Therefore, whereas previously during the days of fasting and purification, he recalled the ancestor's dwelling and his laughter and speech, fearing only that it would be insufficient to move him, now it is dimly as though he beholds his very form and bearing; whereas formerly he recalled what the ancestor relished and delighted in, worrying only that it would be insufficient to bring him to accept the offering, now in solemn awe it is as though he hears his very voice. Is this not how the moving power of the music reaches and draws near the spirit of the former king? Nor is this all. The ode says: "The large bells and drums ring out in succession; the myriad dances are grandly performed. We have our admirable guests—do they not also feel at ease and pleased?" Thus the music of the Shang people moved not only the spirits, but men as well. It also says: "From of old, in ancient times, the former people set the example: mild and reverent morning and evening, conducting the service with respect." Thus in the sacrifices of the Shang people, they valued not merely sound, but reverence even more. Ah! Music complete and sincere reverence cultivated—was it not by this that they communicated between the unseen and the manifest, and brought harmony to spirits and men alike?

Therefore, acting upon the wishes of the feudal lords, he conducted the covenant at You. Not only did Song and Lu, which commanded popular esteem, arrive, but even Chen and Zheng, which had harbored doubts and duplicity, also came. They were at once united in mind in honoring the King, arousing sentiments like the Yangtze and Han rivers flowing in homage to the sea; and they were likewise united in mind in cooperating with the霸 (Hegemon), stirring thoughts of the fundamental root and source of water and wood. Once the royal prestige was revitalized, the hegemonic enterprise was consequently accomplished; Huan of Qi's commitment to honoring the King may truly be called diligent!

Thereafter, at Shouzhi there was the righteous act of establishing the great foundation [the royal heir], and at Tao there was the achievement of stabilizing the overall situation. When Zai Kong received the royal mandate to bestow sacrificial meat, Duke Huan happened to be leading the feudal lords to hold the meeting at Kuiqiu. He seated Kong in the superior position, remaining modest and yielding after receiving added commendation and a bestowal of rank; he bowed twice from below, remaining apprehensive in his reply about fear of bringing disgrace upon his sovereign above. The rites of high and low were not transgressed, and the distinctions between superior and inferior were not lost; the royal prohibitions were thereby made bright and clear, and the hegemonic enterprise thereby reached its utmost flourishing. Without Duke Huan's single-minded diligence, how could it have come to this?

The Way by which the sage nurtures the myriad people is great indeed, yet it is nothing more than what is called benevolence. What is benevolence? It is the mind of Heaven and Earth in giving life to things, which human beings receive in order to live. When the sage embodies the mind of Heaven and Earth in giving life to things so as to nurture the myriad people, how could there be any among the myriad people who do not receive his beneficence and find their proper place? Allow me to expound upon this. That by which Heaven and Earth give life to human beings certainly desires to cause them to find their proper place; yet though they are able to give them life, causing them to find their proper place depends upon the sage. When a sage appears, Heaven necessarily charges him to act as the ruler of the myriad states and to serve as the sovereign and teacher of thehundreds of millions of people, desiring only that he embody this mind so as to govern things on Heaven’s behalf. Since that by which Heaven charges the sage is such as this, then without this benevolence, by what means could the sage govern things on Heaven’s behalf? 日星之烜赫不啻如雲漢之昭回然求其要則

蘊奧精微之旨究之竊恐未至姑述其槩以復明

第二問
趙恢

第二問
趙恢
translation_en:
Thus these two books are truly a precious mirror for self-cultivation and governance, and indeed do not go beyond the invariable human relationships of daily life. This being so, the books of the Two Sages succeed one another in turn, handing down models established for the world in this manner; they are truly what is described as shining as brilliantly as the sun and stars, and no less than the radiant revolving of the Milky Way. Yet if one seeks their essential point, it lies in ensuring that the good have that by which they are encouraged and the evil have that by which they are warned, with nothing that is not done to create blessings for the people. Great indeed are the august words! Unified indeed is the august mind! Is this not truly what is called "establishing the mind for Heaven and Earth, establishing destiny for the living people, continuing the lost learning for past sages, and opening up great peace for ten thousand generations"? Humble as I am, having received the grace of the court's education, although I have thoroughly read and carefully savored the books of the Two Sages, in investigating their profound and subtle purport I privately fear I have not yet reached the mark. I tentatively set forth their general outline in reply to your brilliant question, not knowing whether it is right or not. I would be most fortunate if Your Reverences would pardon my rash and unpolished words, advance me, and instruct me.

Question Two
Zhao Hui 趙恢

Sang Hongyang 桑弘羊 and Wang Anshi 王安石 merely knew how to press urgently for taxes and levies to meet the needs of the moment, yet they did not know how to take virtue as the foundation. As for Someone like Liu Yan 劉晏, did he not come close to the mark? Consider his words: "In managing finances, one must give priority to nourishing the people; those who deliberate on great affairs do not calculate minor expenses," as well as his arguments that "receipts and disbursements must be entrusted to men of the scholar class, and when officials are numerous, the people are harassed"—all of these are worthy of emulation. If those who manage finances in later times take the teachings of Zengzi 曾子 as their foundation and consult the words of Liu Yan in practice, then the foundation of the state will be secure and state expenditures will be sufficient. No discourse could be more thoroughly appropriate than this, and I venture to offer it up. May the Examiners pardon my lack of discernment and instruct me; I would be most fortunate.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Our Dynasty has long established examination categories to select scholars and promote Great Peace down to the present day. All quarters and myriad states look up to the moral transformation, and the enterprise of Great Peace is indeed such as has never existed since antiquity. In the spring of the eighth year of the Xuande era (1433), the Auxiliary Ministry of Rites conducted the Metropolitan Examination for the tribute scholars presented from across the realm. The Minister, your servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, petitioned for the appointment of Examiners; His Majesty commanded the Junior Guardian, your servant [Huang] Huai 黃淮, to serve, and your servant [Wang] Zhi 王直 was also unworthily included among them. One hundred of the finest candidates were selected, all representing the supreme choice of the age. Your servant Zhi has previously argued that Heaven entrusts these people to the ruler so that he may govern and instruct them. Yet the completion of this governance and instruction necessarily relies upon the worthy talents of the realm. It is just like the flying dragon in the heavens: to rain upon the earth below and moisten the myriad things, the wind must rise and the clouds must follow it. Therefore, Heaven brings forth worthies across the realm for the ruler's sake; the ruler perfects their talents and promotes and employs them, enabling them to achieve their merits in lofty and resplendent great deeds and flourishing accomplishments. It was thus in the ages of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. Under the August Ming, sage succeeds sage, their virtue equaling that of Yao and Shun, while the breadth of the realm surpasses theirs…
